Why Are We Doing This?

Set aside the cooling drinks and your laptops for a minute. Today, my aim is to give you a lightning-fast calculus review, and then we’re going to apply it to something that will actually get your heart racing. We are going to figure out how to extract real, physical insights—like G-force acceleration and total track distance—from a messy, real-world dataset where we don’t even have a neat mathematical equation to start with. We’re going to see how the concepts of calculus apply to real life, even when the functions are crazy and unpredictable.

TL;DR — Key Takeaways

We reviewed the graphical intuition behind calculus: taking a derivative means finding the slope of a curve, and taking an integral means finding the area under a curve. We then applied these concepts to a real-world dataset of a rally car’s speed over time. By numerically differentiating the speed (calculating the slope between data points), we found the driver experienced accelerations around 1\text{G}. By numerically integrating the speed (calculating the area under the curve, which we quickly estimated using a mental rectangle), we found the total track length was about 7 kilometers.

Learning Objectives

By the end of these notes, you should be able to:

  • Explain differentiation graphically as the local slope of a function.

  • Explain integration graphically as the accumulated area under a function.

  • Convert speed data from km/h to m/s to ensure consistent SI units for acceleration.

  • Estimate the definite integral of a noisy, real-world dataset using a visual average.

  • Apply Python functions like np.gradient and cumulative_trapezoid to numerically differentiate and integrate tabular data.

Before You Start

You should be comfortable with basic algebra, the equation of a straight line (y = mx + b), and the concept of rise-over-run for calculating slopes. It also helps to remember your basic kinematics from physics: acceleration is the rate of change of speed (the derivative), and displacement is the accumulation of speed over time (the integral).

A Very Fast Calculus Review

Let’s do a really, really quick review of the sort of stuff your normal calculus classes have hopefully taught you. We’re going to wrap this up in about fifteen minutes so we can get to the exciting stuff.

Differentiation: Finding the Slope

Before you knew anything about calculus, if I asked you what it meant to "differentiate" a function, you might have had no idea. But having seen it before, how do we explain it graphically?

Taking the derivative of a function means finding its rate of change, or graphically, its slope.

Let’s look at a simple polynomial function where our variable is time, t: \begin{equation} f(t) = at^2 + bt + c \tag{1} \end{equation}

If we want to take the derivative of this whole thing, the rules of calculus tell us we can break it up and take the derivative of each term individually. Let’s look at them one by one to build our graphical intuition.

1. The constant term (c): This is a really boring function. If we plot f(t) = c, it’s just a flat, horizontal line staying put at the value c. Because it’s flat, there is no slope anywhere. The slope is zero everywhere. Therefore, the derivative of a constant is 0.

2. The linear term (bt): This is a line that passes through the origin. Regardless of where you are along this line, the steepness never changes. It has a constant slope of b. Therefore, the derivative of bt is simply b.

3. The quadratic term (at^2): This plots as a parabola. If we look at the slope at the very bottom of the parabola (t=0), it’s flat—zero slope. But if we take a step to the right, we see some positive slope. If we take another step to the right, the curve is even steeper. As time increases, the slope keeps increasing at a constant rate.

It turns out that if you plot those slopes, they form a straight line. The rule you probably learned in calculus is that you pull the exponent down in front and subtract one from the power. So, the 2 comes down, and t^2 becomes t^1: \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}(at^2) = 2at \tag{2} \end{equation}

Putting it all together, the derivative of our original function is: \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}(at^2 + bt + c) = 2at + b + 0 \tag{3} \end{equation}

Integration: Finding the Area

Integration is like the evil twin of differentiation. It’s not actually any more evil, it’s just the exact opposite operation.

If differentiation is finding the slope, what is integration? Graphically, integrating a function means quantifying the area under the curve.

Let’s take the result we just got, f(t) = 2at + b, and integrate it to see if we get our original function back. Again, we can split it into parts.

1. Integrating the constant (b): If we plot a flat line at height b, and we want the area under it from time 0 to time t, we are just calculating the area of a rectangle. The width is t and the height is b. \begin{equation} \text{Area} = \text{width} \times \text{height} = t \times b = bt \tag{4} \end{equation}

2. Integrating the linear term (2at): If we plot 2at, we get a straight line starting at the origin and going up. The area under this line forms a triangle. Let’s say we want the area from time 0 to time t. The base of our triangle is t, and the height of the triangle at that time is 2at. The formula for the area of a triangle is half the base times the height: \begin{equation} \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times (t) \times (2at) = at^2 \tag{5} \end{equation}

Look at that! We got at^2 + bt back. But wait, what about the c?

When we integrate, we are accumulating area. But nobody explicitly told us we *had* to start measuring our area from t=0. It’s a free country! What if I decided to be a rebel and start calculating my area from t=2? Because the starting point isn’t strictly defined unless we specify bounds, there could be some initial offset area. This is why, in calculus, you always tack on a constant of integration, C.

\begin{equation} \int (2at + b) \, dt = at^2 + bt + C \tag{6} \end{equation}

These operations are perfectly consistent and equivalent. That’s the boring stuff out of the way. Now, let’s look at a real-world application.

Real-World Data: The Rally Car

I hope nobody gets motion sick easily. I found this gameplay video of DiRT Rally 2.0. The driver is going absolutely crazy on this winding dirt path, hitting speeds of 160 km/h (about 100 mph). I don’t know why I thought this was a good idea to analyze, but it seemed like a great idea last night.

I wanted to know how the speedometer reading changed over time. Now, I like you all enough that I *could* have spent hours pausing the video every single second to write down the speed manually. But instead, I used AI.

It took a few tries, and I had to use a paid model (I pay the 20 bucks a month so I can do this kind of stuff), but it worked! We extracted the speed in kilometers per hour (km/h) for every second of the race.

Look at this graph. It looks like a mess. It doesn’t look like any clean polynomial function at^2 + bt + c that you’ve ever seen in a math class.

So, what useful quantitative insights can we gain from this? Two things come to mind: 1. Acceleration: How many Gs is this driver feeling? Are they going to black out like Maverick in Top Gun? 2. Displacement: How long is this race track?

Differentiating Real Data: Acceleration

Let’s tackle acceleration first. If you want to be a fighter pilot or an astronaut, you care about G-force. We know that acceleration is the derivative of speed with respect to time.

But before we take any derivatives, we need to fix our units. We want to compare the driver’s acceleration to standard gravity (1\text{G} \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s\textsuperscript{2}}). Right now, our speed is in km/h. We need it in meters per second (m/s).

How do we convert 100 km/h into m/s?

We need to convert kilometers to meters (multiply by 1000) and hours to seconds (divide by 3600).

Let’s set up the conversion: \begin{align} \text{Speed (m/s)} &= \text{Speed (km/h)} \times \left( \frac{1000 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ km}} \right) \times \left( \frac{1 \text{ hr}}{3600 \text{ s}} \right) \nonumber \\ &= \text{Speed (km/h)} \times \left( \frac{10}{36} \right) \end{align}

Now we have our speed in m/s. But how do we take the derivative of this messy data? We don’t have an equation to use our exponent rules on. If we tried to fit a polynomial to this, we’d need thousands of terms. I don’t recommend it.

Remember our graphical definition: the derivative is just the slope! To find the acceleration at any given second, we just look at the data points around it and calculate the slope (rise over run). We draw a tangent line that follows the local rate of change.

Let’s verify our units. Slope is rise over run. The "rise" is the change in speed (m/s). The "run" is the change in time (s). \begin{equation} \text{Acceleration} = \frac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \frac{\text{m/s}}{\text{s}} = \text{m/s}^2 \tag{7} \end{equation} The units are perfectly kosher.

Looking at the acceleration plot, it’s jumping around a lot. But lucky for the driver, the acceleration rarely exceeds 9.8 \text{ m/s\textsuperscript{2}}. This means the driver is experiencing about 1\text{G} of acceleration. So, while we would probably be very scared to be in the passenger seat, and we might throw up, we aren’t going to black out.

Key Takeaway

When you have real-world tabular data instead of a mathematical function, you can find the derivative numerically by calculating the slope (rise over run) between adjacent data points.

Integrating Real Data: Displacement

Now, how far did the car actually travel?

In physics, to go from displacement to speed, you take the derivative. Therefore, to go from speed to displacement, we must do the opposite: integrate the speed with respect to time.

Graphically, this means finding the area under our messy speed curve.

Because the shape is so crazy, we can’t just use a simple triangle or rectangle formula for the whole thing. The beauty of numerical integration is that we can break this crazy shape up into a bunch of tiny, 1-second-wide vertical strips. If the strips are narrow enough, they look like rectangles.

For example, if the car is going 10 \text{ m/s} for 1 \text{ second}, the area of that strip is 10 \text{ m/s} \times 1 \text{ s} = 10 \text{ meters}. Even when the driver hits the brakes and decelerates, they are still moving forward (speed is positive), so we keep adding positive area to our total displacement.

We can have Python do this strip-by-strip addition for us (which we will see in the code section below), but there is a really quick way to estimate this manually.

Without adding up 230 individual rectangles, how can we quickly estimate the total area under this jagged curve?

We can mentally flatten the curve into a single giant rectangle by guessing the average speed.

Just by looking at the graph, you can mentally draw a horizontal line where you think the average speed is. The speed fluctuates up and down, but it seems to average out around 30 \text{ m/s}.

Instead of a crazy shape, we now just have one big rectangle.

  • Height (Average Speed): \approx 30 \text{ m/s}

  • Width (Time Duration): The race starts a few seconds in and ends a bit before 230s, so let’s call it \approx 220 \text{ s}.

\begin{equation} \text{Total Displacement} \approx 30 \text{ m/s} \times 220 \text{ s} = 6600 \text{ meters} \tag{8} \end{equation}

Since this is a rough estimation, we can round that up to about 7000 \text{ meters}, or 7 \text{ km}.

Key Takeaway

You can quickly estimate the definite integral of a noisy dataset by approximating the area as a single rectangle: multiply the estimated average height by the total width.

The Python Implementation

While mental math is great for estimations, we can use Python to do the rigorous numerical calculus for us. I wrote two scripts to analyze this data.

The first script calculates the displacement using scipy.integrate.cumulative_trapezoid. This function does exactly what we discussed: it breaks the area under the curve into tiny shapes (trapezoids, which are slightly more accurate than rectangles) and adds them up step-by-step. It also generates a cool frame-by-frame animation of the race progress.

Show Python code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import cv2
import os
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid

# 1. Load the data
df = pd.read_csv('260323 rally car data.csv')

# 2. Convert km/h to km/s
df['Speed (km/s)'] = df['Speed (km/h)'] / 3600.0

# 3. Calculate displacement (numerical integral)
df['Displacement (km)'] = cumulative_trapezoid(df['Speed (km/s)'], df['Time (s)'], initial=0)

# 4. Define constant for Speed Y-axis (for consistent visual scale)
max_speed_global = df['Speed (km/s)'].max() * 1.1

if not os.path.exists('dynamic_frames'):
    os.makedirs('dynamic_frames')

frame_files = []

# 5. Generate frames with dynamic ranges
for t_idx in range(1, len(df)):
    t_val = df.iloc[t_idx]['Time (s)']
    current_df = df.iloc[:t_idx+1]
    
    # Dynamic Limits
    # X-axis: starts at 10, grows with current time
    x_limit = max(10, t_val)
    # Displacement Y-axis: starts at 0.1, grows with max displacement seen so far
    current_max_disp = current_df['Displacement (km)'].max()
    y_limit_disp = max(0.1, current_max_disp * 1.1)
    
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(8, 8))
    
    # Top Graph: Speed vs Time
    ax1.plot(current_df['Time (s)'], current_df['Speed (km/s)'], color='blue')
    ax1.fill_between(current_df['Time (s)'], current_df['Speed (km/s)'], color='blue', alpha=0.3)
    ax1.set_ylabel('Speed (km/s)')
    ax1.set_xlim(0, x_limit)
    ax1.set_ylim(0, max_speed_global)
    ax1.set_title(f'Rally Car Progress - Time: {t_val}s')
    ax1.grid(True)
    
    # Bottom Graph: Displacement vs Time
    ax2.plot(current_df['Time (s)'], current_df['Displacement (km)'], color='red')
    ax2.set_xlabel('Time (s)')
    ax2.set_ylabel('Displacement (km)')
    ax2.set_xlim(0, x_limit)
    ax2.set_ylim(0, y_limit_disp)
    ax2.grid(True)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    filename = f'dynamic_frames/frame_{t_idx:03d}.png'
    plt.savefig(filename)
    frame_files.append(filename)
    plt.close()

# 6. Compile images into a single video
output_video = 'rally_car_dynamic_animation.mp4'
frame = cv2.imread(frame_files[0])
height, width, layers = frame.shape
fourcc = cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'mp4v')
video = cv2.VideoWriter(output_video, fourcc, 10, (width, height))

for image_file in frame_files:
    video.write(cv2.imread(image_file))

video.release()

The second script does the heavy lifting for our static plots. It uses np.gradient to find the numerical derivative (the acceleration) by calculating the central difference (slope) between adjacent points. It also plots the tangent lines we looked at earlier.

Show Python code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid

# 1. Load the data from the CSV file
df = pd.read_csv('260323 rally car data.csv')

# 2. Convert speed from km/h to m/s
df['Speed (m/s)'] = df['Speed (km/h)'] / 3.6

# 3. Calculate acceleration (m/s^2) using numerical gradient
# np.gradient uses second-order accurate central differences
df['Acceleration (m/s^2)'] = np.gradient(df['Speed (m/s)'], df['Time (s)'])

# 4. Calculate displacement (m) using numerical integration (trapezoidal rule)
# We assume the car starts at displacement = 0
df['Displacement (m)'] = cumulative_trapezoid(df['Speed (m/s)'], df['Time (s)'], initial=0)

# Helper variables for plotting
time = df['Time (s)']
speed_ms = df['Speed (m/s)']
accel = df['Acceleration (m/s^2)']
displacement = df['Displacement (m)']
mask_10s = (time % 10 == 0)

# --- Plot 1: Speed (km/h) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, df['Speed (km/h)'], label='Speed (km/h)', color='blue')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Speed (km/h)')
plt.title('Rally Car Speed (km/h) vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('speed_kmh.png')

# --- Plot 2: Speed (m/s) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, speed_ms, label='Speed (m/s)', color='red')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Speed (m/s)')
plt.title('Rally Car Speed (m/s) vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('speed_ms.png')

# --- Plot 3: Acceleration (m/s^2) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
# All points: empty circles connected by lines
plt.plot(time, accel, color='green', marker='o', markerfacecolor='none', 
         markeredgecolor='green', markersize=4, linestyle='-', label='Acceleration')
# 10s intervals: black filled circles
plt.plot(time[mask_10s], accel[mask_10s], color='black', marker='o', 
         markerfacecolor='black', linestyle='None', label='Intervals (10s)')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Acceleration (m/s$^{2}$)')
plt.title('Rally Car Acceleration vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('acceleration_vs_time.png')

# --- Plot 4: Speed (m/s) with Tangent Line Segments ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, speed_ms, color='red', label='Speed (m/s)', alpha=0.6)
dt_seg = 2.5 # Length of tangent segment for visualization
for t0 in time[mask_10s]:
    idx = df[df['Time (s)'] == t0].index[0]
    v0 = speed_ms[idx]
    a0 = accel[idx]
    
    # Define tangent line: v = a0*(t - t0) + v0
    t_seg = np.array([t0 - dt_seg, t0 + dt_seg])
    v_seg = a0 * (t_seg - t0) + v0
    
    plt.plot(t_seg, v_seg, color='black', linewidth=1.5)
    plt.plot(t0, v0, marker='o', color='black', markerfacecolor='black')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Speed (m/s)')
plt.title('Speed (m/s) with Tangent Line Segments (every 10s)')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('speed_ms_with_tangents.png')

# --- Plot 5: Displacement (m) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, displacement, color='purple', label='Displacement (m)')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Displacement (m)')
plt.title('Rally Car Displacement (Distance Travelled) vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('displacement_vs_time.png')

print(f"Total distance travelled: {displacement.iloc[-1]:.2f} meters.")
Key Terms
Derivative

The rate of change of a function, represented graphically as the slope of the curve at a given point.

Integral

The accumulation of a quantity over time, represented graphically as the area under the curve.

Constant of Integration (C)

An arbitrary constant added to the result of an indefinite integral to account for the unknown starting offset.

Numerical Differentiation

Estimating the derivative of a dataset by calculating the slope (rise over run) between discrete data points.

Numerical Integration

Estimating the integral of a dataset by breaking the area under the curve into small geometric shapes (like rectangles or trapezoids) and summing their areas.
